insider_note: The book's own printed working reaches the same value through (t²−1)/(1+t²), a sign-flipped version of the split used here — either route lands on π(π−2)/2, so use whichever split is faster to remember.

steps.label: Apply the King's property
steps.margin_note: First two marks. sin³ carries the same sign rule as sin — check it does not flip.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π − x) = sinx, so sin³(π − x) = sin³x — cubing an unchanged quantity changes nothing.
steps.why: sin(π − x) = sinx, so sin³(π − x) = sin³x, and cos²(π − x) = cos²x as before — only the x in the numerator changes to π − x, exactly the setup the addition step needs.

steps.label: Add and expand sin³x
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. Expanding sin³x is what makes the cosx = t substitution possible in the next step.
steps.memory_tip: sin³x = sin²x·sinx = (1 − cos²x)sinx — always split an odd power of sine this way before substituting cosx = t.
steps.why: sin³x = sin²x·sinx = (1 − cos²x)sinx, which turns the integral into a function of cosx multiplied by sinx dx — exactly the form the substitution cosx = t needs.
common_mistakes: Leaving sin³x unexpanded, which blocks the cosx = t substitution.
Writing sin²x as 1 + cos²x instead of 1 − cos²x.

steps.label: Substitute cosx = t and integrate
steps.margin_note: Two marks for the substitution and splitting the resulting fraction.
steps.memory_tip: (1 − t²)/(1 + t²) always splits as 2/(1 + t²) − 1 — memorise this identity, it appears repeatedly in this chapter.
lines: Put cosx = t ⇒ sinx dx = −dt. x = 0
steps.why: Splitting (1 − t²)/(1 + t²) as 2/(1 + t²) − 1 turns the integrand into two pieces with easy antiderivatives — Tan⁻¹t and t itself.
common_mistakes: Writing (1 − t²)/(1 + t²) as 1 − t²/(1 + t²) and then failing to combine terms correctly.
A sign slip when flipping the limits.

steps.label: Evaluate the limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. π(π − 2)/2 is the box the examiner looks for.
steps.memory_tip: 2Tan⁻¹(1) = π/2 and 2Tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/2 — the same angle pair as every King's-property question in this chapter.
steps.why: 2Tan⁻¹(1) = π/2 and 2Tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/2; substituting both endpoints and simplifying leaves π − 2 inside the bracket, which is then halved by the outer π/2.
common_mistakes: Dropping the −t / +t terms at the two limits.
Writing the final answer as π²/2 − π/2 instead of the equivalent π(π − 2)/2.
